item.title: Can We Really Learn to Slow Down Time?
item.description:
Attention

Can We Really Learn to Slow Down Time?

What perception neuroscience tells us about attention, belief, and reality.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • The brain filters and interprets reality rather than just recording it, so there is no objective "out there."
  • Our beliefs and expectations influence what we perceive as possible, including limiting how we see ourselves.
  • Meditation, training, and new experiences can revise deeply embedded beliefs to allow for a person to change.

Most of us go through life assuming that what we see around us is reality. That’s a table. There’s a tree. We hear words spoken to us. An hour passes on the clock we see. Our brain takes in all of this, and we experience it. Except, from the standpoint of neuroscience, that’s not really what’s happening. In fact, the brain doesn’t give us an unedited picture of the world. It filters a remarkable amount of information, picks out what it thinks matters, combines that with what we already know and expect, and gives us something closer to a working model of reality. Yikes! You mean there’s nothing “out there” to be perceived other than our own perceptions?

Pretty much yes, in some sense, that's a true statement, and it all starts with our senses. Human vision detects only a small portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Our hearing also has limits. Even with the things our senses can detect, most never get to our conscious awareness. The brain must be selective, otherwise we’d be overwhelmed by information and pretty much incapable of doing anything. Then something even more astounding happens. What we expect to see can influence what we actually perceive. Neuroscience research has shown that prior expectations affect the brain’s processing of incoming information delivered by the senses. The brain continually pulls out previous experiences to make predictions about what’s out there and compares those with the information coming in.

Role of Expectations and Beliefs in Shaping Perception

So perception isn’t just information coming from the outside world into the brain. There’s traffic, like you would see on a massive highway, going in both directions. Our prior experiences, expectations and learned beliefs all become part of that traffic. They influence what we notice and how we interpret what we run into in our daily lives.

Source: johnhain/Pixabay

Think about beliefs rattling around in your brain for years: I’m not a good writer. I’m not good at math. I’m not popular. I’m just the way I am, and too old to learn that. I don’t belong with those people. I’m not good enough. After enough repetition, we stop experiencing these statements as beliefs. To us, they become facts about who we think we are—and how we show up in the world. This is where adding training and exposure to the mix gets interesting. If our brains use previous experience to interpret what’s possible right now, then serving up to the brain brand new experiences can start to change the predictions it makes. But don’t believe that you can just talk yourself into the new belief becoming your reality. The way to do it is to practice something, expose yourself to people and environments that are the counterfactuals of your assumptions, and accumulate evidence that our old model is incomplete. Do that, and you can rid yourself of that pesky recurring thought, “I’m not enough."

Moreover, meditation can help a lot with this, by training brain activity to operate on new patterns. For example, there’s a part of the brain called the “default mode network." It’s a group of connected areas in the brain that becomes really active when our attention turns inward, such as when we’re thinking about ourselves, remembering our past, imagining our future, or replaying the ongoing story we carry about who we are. Research suggests that meditation can change both the activity within this network and how its different regions communicate with one another. Said another way, with training, we may be able to become a little less captive to the running commentary in our heads about who we are.

Subjective vs. Objective Time Perception

And then there’s the issue of time. We live our lives in physical bodies which exist in space and time, and our brains organize how and what we experience accordingly. Events happen somewhere. One thing happens before another. We remember the past and wonder about the future. This ordering the brain does is essential for us to function in the world. But clock time and psychological time are two very different things. Five minutes waiting for life-altering medical news doesn’t pass in the same way as five minutes having dinner with your loved ones. Research confirms what we already know from experience: subjective time is surprisingly elastic. Attention, emotion, motivation, and what we’re doing all change how long an interval of time feels.

That suggests we have some ability to influence our experience of time. When we focus our attention on time itself, time feels like it's passing more slowly. When we’re not focusing on anything, like being absorbed in a project or conversation, it feels like it's passing more quickly. Research on subjective time has found that directing our attention toward time can expand its perceived duration, while directing attention away from it can contract it.

Influencing the Perception of Time and Reality

Which gives us something really practical to work with. If I want an anticipated experience to feel even more pleasurable while you’re living it, deliberately bring your attention back to what’s happening in the moment: the conversation, the music, the feeling of a breeze blowing on your skin, the face you see across the table. If we want an unpleasant time in our lives to pass faster, absorb yourself doing something else. We can also become more conscious of the assumptions we have about our lives. Maybe some of what we experience as the fixed nature of reality is instead only the structure through which our human brains have learned to perceive it.

Neuroscience doesn’t suggest we can think our way completely outside the bounds of physical time or change the laws of physics. But it does tell us something valuable: our experience of reality is constructed by us, selected by us, and surprisingly changeable—by us. We may not be able to change reality with a snap of our fingers. But by focusing our attention and practicing, we can change some of the filters through which we experience it. And that may give us a lot more room to become a different person than our old beliefs told us we were, or insisted we had to be.

item.title: Why We Put Things Off
item.description:
Procrastination

Why We Put Things Off

Understand the varieties and causes of procrastination.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination is a very common behavior that negatively affects both academic and everyday functioning.
  • While not technically a disorder, procrastination may reflect maladaptive personality processes.
  • Perfectionism paradoxically leads to procrastination from fear of not meeting high standards.

Procrastination, from the Latin word for “tomorrow” (as in, “I’ll get to it tomorrow”), is perhaps the most common behavioral affliction in the modern world. As example, around 90% of college students report some procrastination tendencies and around 25% have procrastination tendencies severe enough to make it very difficult for them to ever attain a degree. In the everyday (as opposed to academic) world, an almost universal form of procrastination involves inability to get rid of clutter, with the most severe manifestation qualifying as hoarding. Other everyday forms of procrastination involve such things as putting off potentially difficult conversations, delaying paying bills, not completing job assignments, etc.

In calling procrastination an “affliction,” I mean to indicate that it is an avoidance behavior that creates undesired consequences for the procrastinator, assuming that most procrastinators would prefer not to get in academic trouble, have their cars repossessed, get fired, etc. On the other hand, procrastination itself does not qualify as a psychiatric disorder, although obviously there are some psychiatric disorders, most typically depression, for which procrastination is a major symptom.

There are obviously many possible explanations for why people procrastinate, and at 1,000 words (the recommended max for this post) I cannot mention all of them. I will briefly discuss a few major causes and then finish up with a discussion of some strategies for avoiding or lessening procrastination tendencies.

Causes of Procrastination

In looking at the major causes of procrastination, it is important to keep in mind that someone could have two or more factors operating in a specific procrastination example. Furthermore, procrastination tends to be time- and task-specific, with the possibility that a person can be a procrastinator one day or with one task and a non-procrastinator on another day or a different task.

1. Demoralization

A common cause of procrastination is feeling overwhelmed by the size of a project. A typical example would be a home in a serious state of clutter. The person faced with such a situation may feel they lack the self-efficacy to complete such a major task, and so they are intimidated from even starting. A Finnish neuroscientist, Dr. Aino Mäkinen, terms this “decision loop paralysis,” in which the brain begins a task but becomes overwhelmed evaluating too many options at once, and shuts down.

2. Perfectionism

While the first cause, demoralization, reflects a lack of confidence in one’s ability to succeed in a challenging task, the second cause, perfectionism, reflects, paradoxically, a high estimation of one’s ability to succeed. The reason why this results in procrastination is because the procrastinator needs the end product (such as a publication) to meet their self-imposed high standards, and fear of not meeting that standard creates crippling anxiety.

3. Distractibility

Many tasks subject to procrastination require sustained effort over a period of time. Many procrastinators, especially those who have a dysregulation condition such as ADHD, are easily distracted and lack the ability to sustain their focus over the length of time needed to complete the task. A modern contributor to such distractibility is the ever-present cell phone, which creates a constant temptation to engage in enjoyable diversions.

4. Demotivation

Tasks subject to procrastination are often things that are not exactly enjoyable but which one does because they serve an important purpose. On occasion, one finds oneself working on a task that serves a purpose (such as living up to someone else’s expectations) that is not very important to oneself. A variant of this is when the project started out being important, but at some point it becomes non-important or even repugnant. When that is the case, one may unconsciously sabotage the project by procrastinating without making a conscious decision to end it.

Methods for Reducing Procrastination

There are many ways to stop procrastinating but, again for space considerations, I shall only list a few of them.

1. The Finnish Method

A logical outgrowth of the concept of ”decision loop paralysis” is to break a major task up into smaller micro tasks. In terms of decluttering, for example, rather than attempt to tackle the whole task, it is useful to resolve to do a different small task (such as straightening the kitchen counter) that should only take a few minutes every day. As these accumulate, becoming more organized can become a habit, and what seems an overwhelming goal may become relatively easy to attain and maintain.

2. Accept Imperfection

As a former procrastinator driven by fear of having my writing viewed negatively, I found that Rational Emotive Therapy (a form of CBT that I have written about as having helped with my emotional development) helped me to become a relatively prolific author. The trick is to attack the anxiety that stems from producing drek (Yiddish for crap) by asking oneself questions such as: (a) “where is it written that only other people have the right to produce drek?”, and (b) “why is it awful if someone might think that my writing is drek?” Once one comes to accept that it is OK to be imperfect will one become able to just do things without worrying about how they might be judged.

3. Bartleby’s Approach

In Herman Melville’s 1853 novella “Bartleby the Scrivener,” the protagonist one day announces “I prefer not to” when asked to scriven (copy by hand) a legal document. Bartleby takes it to extremes (he eventually prefers not to do everything, including eat) but the basic idea—that it is OK to end an activity one hates—has some validity. The problem is that serial procrastinators are too quick to reach that conclusion over and over again. Thus it is important to decide if abandoning a project reflects one’s true values or is rather a maladaptive avoidance mechanism that expresses, rather than ends, procrastination.

4. Device Withdrawal

One way to combat procrastination related to internet usage is to adopt a policy of not checking one’s phone or other devices except on widely separated occasions. However, this is easier said than done.

5. Prescription Drugs

For those whose procrastination reflects a dysregulation condition such as ADHD, a solution might be to take a physician-prescribed medication such as methylphenidate (Ritalin).

Conclusion

As I have said to various students of mine (and to myself), “Procrastination is boring. Just do it.”

Copyright Stephen Greenspan.

item.title: How Do We Make Aesthetic Choices?
item.description:
Behavioral Economics

How Do We Make Aesthetic Choices?

Fast instincts and slow reflection both guide our tastes.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • The aesthetics of a product largely determine its first impression on the user.
  • Shoppers constantly balance how good an item looks with how useful it will actually be.
  • Products that are easier for people's minds to process leave a better overall impression.
Source: Free stock photos / Pixabay

Many of us regularly make aesthetic choices. We buy paintings, music, and novels; we visit concerts and galleries. Aesthetic buying refers to buying things just because they are pleasing to the eye, not for their utility. Visually appealing products stimulate the brain’s reward system, triggering dopamine and offering instant gratification. Buying things that look good becomes emotionally satisfying, even if they serve no real purpose.

The buying decision process, in general, involves the interaction of two distinct decision systems (often in conflict with each other): a deliberative system (analytic thinking) and an automatic (impulsive) system. To make good choices, the two systems must work well together to support a person’s actual goals.

When we are calm, the deliberative system guides slow, rational thinking. The impulsive system acts spontaneously without consideration for the broader consequences of the action. The impulsive system is heavily biased toward the present (clicking “Buy Now”). The final decision is based on the relative strength of the impulsive system and the deliberative system.

Aesthetic preference can also be the product of two distinct processes that differ fundamentally in the way the perceiver engages in the processing of the stimulus: gut feeling and aesthetic elaboration (Graf & Landwehr, 2017). People may process aesthetic stimuli not only passively but also actively and elaborately, like when a customer evaluates the interior as well as exterior designs of a car.

In other words, when people encounter an object (cars, bikes, chairs, or iPhones), they can pass an aesthetic judgment spontaneously and quickly, or they can process the object more extensively, which includes reflection and elaboration, before they evaluate it aesthetically. Aesthetic judgments are likely to be qualitatively different depending on which approach is used.

The Clash Between Beauty and Function

Aesthetic choices are based on a trade-off (a battle) between beauty and usefulness. For example, when people approach a car in a showroom or see a new car model in a magazine, their first response will be one of visual attractiveness: “Does this car appeal to me?” But we are also reluctant to spend on such items and tend toward those that appear, above all, to be practical (useful). In this case, the reflective system exerts control over the impulsive system to suppress the urges.

Our attitude formation is often prompted by visual appeal or visual aesthetics. Instinctively, we reach out for attractive things. The human brain processes visual information remarkably quickly. For example, research shows consumers can form opinions about websites within 50 milliseconds of visual exposure (Schlamann, 2026). This rapid assessment determines whether potential customers feel drawn in or deterred before they have consciously evaluated features or benefits.

Product aesthetics create powerful first impressions that influence purchasing decisions through emotional connection rather than rational analysis. When products are visually appealing, consumers perceive them as higher quality, more valuable, and more trustworthy. This explains why well-designed products often command premium pricing even when their functional capabilities match lower-priced alternatives.

Why Simplicity Wins the Sale

In contrast, the deliberative system is typically effortful. This may explain why responses to artwork vary as a function of expertise (their brains decode complex artwork effortlessly). That is why people prefer things that are easy to process; it helps them to allocate limited mental resources in a world with high demand on their attention. The ease of processing (known as cognitive fluency) makes things familiar and is associated with positive evaluations.

In sum, aesthetic judgments critically depend on the perceiver’s processing style that interacts with the ease or diﬃculty of stimulus processing. The aesthetic judgment determines the purchase of expensive items (e.g., furniture), implying that people are likely to have a greater need to think more deeply when encountering aesthetic products.

item.title: Not Everything Needs an Easy Button
item.description:
Career

Not Everything Needs an Easy Button

In the age of AI, embracing challenge is a worthy goal.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • AI is impacting everything from college curriculum to hiring to how people work.
  • Scaffolding skills and learning through challenge are key to the educational process.
  • The skills that make individuals uniquely human are what make them successful in a disrupted world.
Source: charlesdeluvio / Unsplash

You may have seen the news at the start of this academic year that the University of Michigan has decided to withhold grades from some members of the incoming first-year class to support their transition and mental health (Arsenault, 2026).

On the face of it, this might not be a terrible idea. The transition to college from high school is a challenging one. We all know that college-level work is very different from that at most high schools, on top of the critical shifts in identity development as Gomes et al. (2026) and others have noted, as well as challenges of increased freedom, access to people and situations that can be detrimental to one’s well-being, and the overwhelming need to prove oneself. We know that we have a mental health crisis in this country among young people (Mowreader, 2025). Any effort to support their wellbeing should be applauded.

That said, college students have spent the previous 12-plus years in institutions that presumably evaluated their daily and weekly performance using grades. They are experienced with this aspect of the educational process. Certainly, getting an A in college is and should be harder than in high school. Hiding or removing a piece of that evaluative experience doesn’t make the work any less challenging; it simply removes a critical piece of clarity from the equation.

In fact, in my work with young professionals, I often hear that one of the biggest challenges with the transition from college to work and life after college is that they stop receiving grades. They don’t know what A-level work looks like in the workplace or in life. They don’t know how to manage their time and productivity with projects that have no endpoint and don’t come with a syllabus and a grading rubric. The academic structure might be stressful and imperfect, but it is, in fact, all they know.

The bigger point is this: Why do we have this urgency to make everything easier? College is supposed to be hard. Learning is supposed to challenge you. And while, yes, there are aspects of our lives that we should be making easier—access to food, clean drinking water, a sustainable lifestyle, just to name a few—these aren’t what our society is focused on. Instead, it’s about increasing productivity and maximizing time.

We should make access to learning assistance and counseling support in college easier. We should also require people to write their own emails and papers, and learn how to do research and how to show up in relationship with others.

We are being inundated with AI tools, strategies, and yes, way too much slop, in the name of efficiency and productivity. But what happens when, in the process, we lose the essential tools that make us both human and of use?

As Slater (2026) notes, regarding the impact AI is having on entry-level jobs:

Every role that AI absorbs is one that a junior employee would once have learned by doing. The efficiency gain and the training loss are the same decision, viewed from different angles.

The consequences for white-collar professions are already visible. Entry-level hiring at major technology companies has fallen more than 50 percent below pre-pandemic levels. Generative AI doesn’t eliminate entire occupations overnight. Instead, it hollows them out from within, automating 30 or 40 per cent of an employee’s workload, leaving fewer entry-level roles and compressing opportunities for career progression. The result is organisations that get more done with fewer people today, but have fewer ways to train the people they will need tomorrow. This creates a widening gap not just between companies but within them, between a shrinking cadre of AI-fluent senior professionals and a growing population of graduates who cannot get a foot on the ladder that those seniors once climbed.

In our eagerness to “get ahead,” we may soon discover that we have fallen behind to a point from which we cannot recover.

What’s the Alternative?

In this moment, it would behoove us all to consider how we might step away from the easy button. In its simplest form, this means not making the internet the first source of information, scrolling past AI-generated summaries to the source documents, and then taking the time to critically assess the truth of what you are reading. And to do that, you have to have the critical thinking and analysis skills that a rigorous education provides.

The skills this moment needs are those that make us uniquely human: relationship-building, interpersonal communication, critical assessment, and the ability to reflect and learn. This is why asking for and providing more feedback, not less—to our students, to each other—is so important. Feedback gives us the information we need so we can keep progressing as students, as professionals, and as humans. It is one of the most important learning and relationship-building tools we possess, and no technology is required to deploy it.

Education has always been about scaffolding skills. We learn to solve the easy problems first, so we have the tools to solve the more difficult ones later. This is true for education, for work, and for life. Removing those early steps rarely results in a better product or a better person. And so, sure, hiding student grades might have the impact of easing the transition into college. And, it might make those students less able to handle greater disappointments or challenges down the road, just as removing entry-level jobs now may result in a less functional workforce later.

In August, MIT released its assessment on the state of AI on their campus, which uncovered some familiar and concerning findings, including that there is a pervasive lack of clarity on AI’s ethical use, the technology is increasing social isolation, and the technology is challenging traditional modes of assessment (Massachusetts, 2026). Anyone working on a college campus is likely nodding along with familiarity. It’s a messy world we’re living in, with no clear direction forward for students or those who would guide them.

The study recommends a set of actions for its campus, including reevaluating the assessment process: “Rather than simply “AI-proof” current methods of assessment, instructors need to revisit what they really want students to know and devise assessments that foster, or even include, the kind of productive struggle that builds durable understanding and mastery.”

That, I think, is the key piece to all this innovation and disruption that is getting lost in the noise. Building our humanity is not about removing obstacles on our paths. It’s about learning how to move beyond the obstacles when they inevitably appear. There is, indeed, productive value in the struggle.

item.title: The Hidden Defenses of Introversion and Extroversion
item.description:
Extroversion

The Hidden Defenses of Introversion and Extroversion

Both silence and chatter can be used as protective shields. Employ them wisely.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Introverts and extroverts process thoughts differently, leading to distinct communication styles.
  • Both types can use behavior to hide, whether through an introvert's silence or an extrovert's fogging.
  • Recognizing introverted and extroverted defense mechanisms allows people to speak openly and build confidence.
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

Carl Jung defined introversion and extroversion as two different ways of processing information. Introversion works with information internally, by quietly reviewing perceptions, ideas, and feelings. Extroverts examine similar material by talking and engaging in conversation. As a natural outcome, introverts tend to speak in bottom lines, reflecting the result of an inner process. Extroverts move verbally toward a conclusion, which may require an extended conversation.

The Cultural Bias

Culture strongly favors extroversion. The thinking is that if you know how to talk and keep talking, then you’re likely intelligent and destined for success. Of course, verbal mastery doesn't correlate with intelligence. However, it is a popular belief. An extrovert may not feel informed about a particular task, yet cite numerous considerations—some relevant, others tangential. I have encountered many introverts who are convinced something is wrong with them. And then, there are the introverts trying to be extroverted. They tend to wander verbally because they are stepping away from their comfort zone of quiet processing.

Two Forms of Invisibility

Both introverts and extroverts can become invisible naturally and unconsciously. The introvert’s invisibility is more obvious because they say nothing. They are not simply introverting when they spend more time in their internal world. If their childhood was marked by abuse, then they likely clung to anonymity as a way to survive. They have more work to do in order to be convinced that there is safety beyond anonymity. An unconscious attachment to invisibility will likely not serve them in their personal or professional lives. Invisibility does not build trust, rapport, or collaboration.

The invisibility extroverts create is more subtle. After all, how invisible can someone be while talking? I call extroverted invisibility fogging. Let’s say the extrovert wants to communicate a single, important message while creating safety. They begin by introducing several ideas not significantly related to the intended message. After communicating their message, they follow up with several other considerations not germane to the topic. Their key point sits among a dozen irrelevant details, making it hard to reject or critique. Of course, it also means that no one quite knows what the speaker wants to convey.

Here’s an example of extroverted fogging:

Bruce tells his family that he’s stepping out of the family business at somewhat of a frantic pace. “Hey, I ran into Pete the other day. I haven’t seen him in years. He’s leaving the insurance field and establishing his own accounting firm. He says his brother George might join him, but knowing George, he won’t be happy working with Pete. It's time for me to step out of our family business. And I’m thinking of spending two weeks in Bermuda. Kate, you were there last year. Do you think early fall is a good time to go? Where do you recommend I stay? You know, I like staying near the water.”

Dismantling Unnecessary Invisibility

For both introverts and extroverts, the goal is to feel more comfortable being visible. Here's how to start:

  • Accept how you protect yourself through invisibility, whether you're an introvert or extrovert.
  • Be gentle with the discovery. (Extroverts can especially be surprised by their use of invisibility.)
  • Honor the need for protection and safety as natural and appropriate.
  • Explore being more intentional about the need to employ invisibility in order to feel safe.
  • Set the stage. Before you speak, let people know how you feel, such as anxious, tentative, shy, or uncertain.
  • Set a boundary. You can make it clear that you don't want any critical feedback.

Being clearer about how you want to be treated as a speaker can yield trustworthy confidence—not founded on making profound remarks or being well-equipped for a debate, but rather due to being honest and self-supporting about how you feel going into the conversation.

item.title: Biology Creates Diversity, Culture Embraces Conformity
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Biology Creates Diversity, Culture Embraces Conformity

Biological and cultural diversity are both essential for human survival.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Genetic variation and DNA mutations drive biological diversity, ensuring species adaptability and survival.
  • Culture provides social structure and identity, but too much conformity risks division and bias.
  • Diverse groups bring varied viewpoints that lead to smarter decisions and stronger cultures.

Statisticians calculate the odds of duplicating an exact “copy" of any one of us are one in 77 trillion. Even in the case of homozygous or identical twins—where two separate individuals share the same genome—epigenetic and environmental influences still sculpt a divergence of distinguishing characteristics.

In all other cases, 23 chromosomes from each parent get thrown into the “nature-nurture blender" to ensure exceptionality, which contributes to diversity and thus species survival. For eons of time, devoid of conscious intent, "mother nature" doggedly continues her expansion of the gene pool, safeguarding the continued existence of all living things.

Succinctly, diversity ensures survival.

Imperfect DNA

Ironically, biology’s life-preserving penchant for diversity is born in “imperfection"; normal cell division isn’t always normal. On a minuscule number of occasions, during mitosis or cell division, DNA fails to duplicate itself perfectly. This translates into mutated genes—mutations that can sparkle with new adaptive life when the opportunity arises in novel environments or environments that have undergone change of some kind. Thus, evolution’s primary criterion of success is met: The gene pool expands, and with it, newly adapted traits assure ongoing reproduction and species survival.

What many consider a classic example of imperfect-but-adaptive gene recombination took place at McGill University in the early 1950s. Experimenters found that exposure to the antibiotic streptomycin killed the vast majority of the bacteria Escherichia coli, except for a few, tail-of-the-distribution mutants that survived the administration of the drug. These few rare, mutant survivors quickly reproduced—new generations of bacteria were spawned every 20 minutes. This newly evolved strain was found to be streptomycin-resistant or immune to the antibiotic. Subsequent generations of this mutant strain actually evolved a dependence on the drug, so that when experimenters withdrew the drug, the preponderance of the now streptomycin-dependent bacteria perished.

Oddly perhaps, biology’s “blunders," or its fondness for diversity, subtly entwines with the environment to select for traits fit for survival.

Cultural Identity and Multiculturalism

Of course, cultures are also diverse. Each culture has a distinct, self-delineating identity that sets it apart from all others. Without these distinctive identities, culture itself would not exist; we’d all be part of a non-differentiated, over-homogenized and outsized melting pot. But cultures are diverse, as reflected in our "cultural membership dues" that are paid in the currency of our customary thinking, feeling, and behaving, which reflects the particular norms, values, and mores of our unique cultural heritage.

Cultural Dividends

Psychologically, culture’s standout advantage is that it reduces the existential uncertainties and anxieties about who we are and what is deemed worthwhile or of value. It bestows upon us a crown of time-tested, well-worn, venerable traditions and customs that take their form in knowable, predictable, purpose-filled ideals, principles, morals, ethics, and mores, all of which grant personal meaning, purpose, and direction to our lives. Because of this, culture tilts us decidedly toward conformity.

Culture’s “Shadowy Side"

Tragically, however, burrowed within culture’s broad basket of advantages lurk some shadowy, bristling disadvantages. With vile muscularity, some individuals and groups cling too tightly, too ethnocentrically, to a narrow mélange of cherry-picked “customs and values" which contorts their subcultures into cults. They “superiorize“ themselves and “inferiorize“ those not of their ethnic, religious, or political persuasion.

Bigoted, crudely dichotomized, "us vs. them" mentalities become the ugly handmaid of exclusion, degradation, and discrimination against people perceived to be outliers, undesirables, or simply those unlike themselves. In its most malignant manifestation, an "us vs. them" mentality is the engine driving and/or justifying actions and sociopolitical movements that often metastasize in violence and warfare—humanity’s disgraced underbelly.

Cultural Diversity

Conversely, as with biology, diversity enriches culture. Indeed, any culture is “on task" when its unique grouping of people adapts to its environmental niche, allowing them to flourish biologically, socially, and emotionally. And, in turn, adaptability nourishes diversity.

For example, social psychologists have long observed a higher quality of outcomes and solutions among heterogeneous groups of decision-makers and problem-solvers, groups comprised of an enriched admixture of gender, race, ethnicity, and ideology. Such diverse groups bring varied perspectives and a broader base of information, which does initially render decision-making a slower, more arduous process. But this initial hurdle is offset by a significant upgrade in the complexity of thinking and evaluating that gets applied to decision-making and problem-solving. The results are better outcomes, higher quality solutions, and adaptive decision-making, as contrasted with the lesser quality of outcomes that tend to characterize homogeneous, “inbred" groups.

Clearly, diversity gifts both biology and culture with life-enhancing quality.

item.title: 5 Things I Learned Moving From Academic to Applied Research
item.description:
Psych Careers

5 Things I Learned Moving From Academic to Applied Research

Here is what surprised me most after moving from academia to consulting.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Applied research generates knowledge about specific populations and contexts that can be put to immediate use.
  • The shift from academic to applied research changes how we think about sampling, ethics, analysis, and impact.
  • Simple analyses can produce the most consequential findings.
Source: RDNE Stock Project / Pexels

Academic research has interested me for most of my life. I was always fascinated by how people come to know, how they sift through information, and how convictions and opinions are formed. It was a natural progression for me to begin my career as a researcher during my undergraduate degree and continue it through my master’s and PhD.

What wasn’t nearly as natural, however, was launching my own research consultancy, Melioscope. I knew that organizations, just like individuals, have their own ways of knowing. I knew that research and knowledge translation could help organizations make decisions and take action based on something approximating the truth, rather than assumptions, intuitions, or incomplete information.

But after a PhD and two postdocs, I discovered that the research process I had become accustomed to was not as easy to translate into the world of applied research as I had expected. In particular, here are five things that surprised me when making the transition:

1. You start with a problem, not a gap in the literature.

In academia, we are often taught that the best research topic is one that is underexplored. While finding a niche may have been relatively simple in the past, today’s academic literature is highly saturated, making it increasingly difficult for emerging academics to feel that their work is truly innovative or making a novel contribution.

With applied research, on the other hand, this is rarely a concern. An organization will rarely choose to address a complex problem simply by exploring what the existing literature says about similar contexts. They want research that reflects their organization, evaluates their programs, and surveys their people.

In this sense, every applied research project has the potential to generate something new: knowledge that is specific to a particular organization, population, program, or problem. The contribution may not be new knowledge for the academic literature, but it is new knowledge for the client—the organization.

2. There often isn’t an ethics board.

Research ethics is a central concern for academic researchers. Every project requires an evaluation of whether participants are being treated fairly and equitably, and whether potential risks and harms have been minimized. Research ethics boards are trained to evaluate these issues and uphold rigorous ethical standards.

In applied research outside the university context, however, there often isn’t an ethics board. The researcher therefore has to be hyper-conscious of ethical standards and maintain university-level ethical principles even when there is no board overseeing the process or sanctioning noncompliance.

In my applied research experience, ethical considerations have sometimes become even more central than in my academic research precisely because there is no committee making sure that I am doing the right, ethical thing. I am the committee.

Source: Vlada Karpovich / Pexels

3. Sometimes, you can study your entire population.

Academic researchers are typically interested in large populations. Children with autism spectrum disorder, individuals with a specific type of cancer, or the experiences of particular marginalized groups are common populations of interest that you might hear about while walking down university hallways. Because it is generally impossible to reach every individual within these populations, a lot of thought has to go into recruiting study participants who are sufficiently representative of the population as a whole. Once the research is conducted, researchers have to determine whether the individuals in their sample are similar enough to the broader population for the findings to be generalized.

One of the most pleasing things about applied research is that sometimes you can recruit the entire population of interest to participate in your study—no generalization required! For example, when evaluating the effects of a new educational program, all of the individuals who participated in the program can potentially be contacted and recruited for a survey. When conducting research within an organization, it may even be possible to invite every single employee to participate.

As the kids say—that’s so satisfying!

4. You can see the impact almost immediately.

Applied research, as the name implies, is put into practical use—often within weeks, and sometimes days, of the final report or debrief. Organizations seeking research or evaluation services are typically facing a complex problem that they are ready to tackle. Research findings can therefore be implemented or incorporated into next steps shortly after the project is completed.

This is in sharp contrast to the pace of impact in academic research. Within universities, the timeline between study conceptualization, implementation, dissemination, and real-world impact can span years or even decades. Some research never culminates in such impact at all.

5. You don’t need fancy analyses to get the most useful results.

Top-tier academic journals increasingly expect manuscripts to include complex statistical analyses. This puts considerable pressure on researchers, especially junior ones, to not only master these analytic skills but also ask complex research questions that require this level of analysis.

In applied research, in sharp contrast, the simplest analyses can sometimes have the greatest impact. Simply knowing the frequency of an experience, understanding differences between two or more groups within an organization, or uncovering associations between two variables can produce consequential findings that propel an organization forward. In applied research, the most sophisticated analysis is not necessarily the most useful one.

What I learned in this transition is that applied research is not a simplified version of academic research; it is a different way of thinking about research altogether. While the commitment to rigour remains, the ultimate goal is different: to understand a specific organization, population, or problem well enough to generate knowledge that can be immediately translated into decisions and meaningful action.
